results.result: Associative learning by pairing whisker signals with olfactory, tail-heating, and gustatory signals leads to reciprocal retrieval of associated signals in PSG mice but not UPSG mice. Olfactory signals induce whisker motion (36.22±2.46° vs 10.20±2.7°), whisker stimulation induces olfactory avoidance (64.82±2.8% vs 48.20±4.62%), tail-heating induces whisker motion (33.63±1.95° vs 8.79±1.66°), whisker stimulation induces tail swing (5.91±0.63s vs 1.13±0.36s), gustatory signals induce whisker motion (35.27±2.62° vs 10.33±1.96°), and whisker stimulation induces tongue licking (4.41±0.54 vs 0.3±0.15 times).
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C34 provide comprehensive behavioral evidence with appropriate statistical analyses (one-way ANOVA, p<0.05 to p<0.0001) demonstrating reciprocal retrieval of associated signals. The data consistently show significant differences between PSG and UPSG groups across all three modality pairings (olfactory, tail, gustatory with whisker), with adequate sample sizes (n=10-17 per group) and clear quantitative measurements.

results.result: Neuronal axons from piriform, S1-Tr, and gustatory cortices project convergently into the barrel cortex after associative learning. GFP-labeled neuron densities are significantly higher in PSG vs UPSG mice in piriform cortex (1.20±0.08 vs 0.22±0.07 ×10³/mm³), S1-Tr cortex (1.55±0.24 vs 0.65±0.18 ×10³/mm³), and gustatory cortex (0.62±0.04 vs 0.20±0.07 ×10³/mm³). Barrel cortical neurons reciprocally project axons and form new synapses onto these cortices, with synapse contact densities significantly elevated in PSG mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C48 provide robust anatomical evidence using retrograde viral tracing (AAV2/retro-CMV-EGFP) and anterograde tracing (AAV2/8-CMV-tdTomato) with appropriate quantification. Statistical analyses show significant differences (p<0.01-0.05, one-way ANOVA) with adequate sample sizes (n=15 cubes from 5 mice for density measurements, n=20 dendrites from 5 mice for synapse contacts). The bidirectional connectivity is well-documented.

results.result: Barrel cortical neurons receive convergent synapse innervations from piriform, S1-Tr, and gustatory cortices after associative learning. Axon bouton densities in barrel cortex are significantly higher in PSG vs UPSG for tdTomato-labeled (1.61±0.14 vs 0.43±0.05 ×10⁴/mm³), GFP-labeled (1.40±0.10 vs 0.38±0.02 ×10⁴/mm³), and BFP-labeled (0.79±0.15 vs 0.17±0.04 ×10⁴/mm³) boutons. Synapse contact densities on barrel cortical dendrites are similarly elevated in PSG mice for all three input sources.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C56 demonstrate convergent synapse innervation using triple-color viral tracing with quantitative confocal microscopy. Statistical analyses are appropriate (p<0.01-0.05, one-way ANOVA) with adequate sample sizes (n=15 cubes from 5 mice for bouton density, n=20 dendrites from 5 mice for synapse contacts). The morphological evidence for associative memory neuron recruitment is convincing.

results.result: Barrel cortical neurons are functionally recruited as associative memory neurons that encode multiple signals after associative learning. The percentage of neurons responding to whisker plus other signals is 64.3% in PSG vs 22% in UPSG mice (p<0.01, χ²-test). Normalized spike frequencies in PSG vs UPSG are elevated for butyl acetate (2.03±0.3 vs 1.19±0.13), tail-heating (2.03±0.31 vs 1.01±0.1), and sucrose (1.39±0.11 vs 0.96±0.07) responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C63 provide functional evidence through in vivo electrophysiology with appropriate statistical tests (χ²-test for proportions, one-way ANOVA for spike frequencies, p<0.01-0.05). Sample sizes are adequate (n=70 neurons from 12 mice in PSG, n=50 neurons from 8 mice in UPSG). The functional recruitment of associative memory neurons encoding multiple modalities is well-demonstrated.

results.result: The barrel cortex functions as a hub enabling indirect signal retrieval among piriform, S1-Tr, and gustatory cortices (second-order associative memory). Tail-heating and sucrose induce olfactory avoidance (~69% and ~67% in PSG vs ~48-50% in UPSG), olfactory and gustatory signals induce tail swing (~5.2-5.4s in PSG vs ~0.8-1.0s in UPSG), and olfactory and tail signals induce tongue licking (~4.3 and ~3.8 times in PSG vs ~0.5-0.6 in UPSG).
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C71 demonstrate second-order associative memory through behavioral experiments showing cross-modal responses that bypass the whisker signal. Statistical analyses are appropriate (p<0.01-0.0001, one-way ANOVA) with adequate sample sizes (n=10-17 per group). The hub function of barrel cortex is supported by both behavioral data and the anatomical connectivity demonstrated in earlier claims.

results.result: Neuroligin-3 knockdown in barrel cortex significantly reduces associative memory formation. Whisker motion amplitudes induced by olfactory (20.11±0.8° vs 32.11±0.65°), tail (18.62±1.26° vs 32.54±1.12°), and gustatory (20.22±0.9° vs 32.54±1.12°) signals are reduced in knockdown vs control mice. Reciprocal responses are similarly impaired: olfactory avoidance (55.63±3.55% vs 68.93±5.07%), tail swing duration (1.56±0.34s vs 4.60±0.37s), and lip licking frequency (1.00±0.26 vs 4.20±0.36 times).
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C80 provide strong causal evidence using shRNA-mediated knockdown with appropriate controls (scrambled shRNA). Statistical analyses are robust (p<0.0001-0.05, one-way ANOVA) with adequate sample sizes (n=10-15 per group). The behavioral impairments are consistent across all tested modalities, supporting the role of neuroligin-3 in associative memory formation.

results.result: Neuroligin-3 knockdown in barrel cortex prevents learning-induced synapse formation from piriform and S1-Tr cortices. Synapse contact densities are significantly reduced in knockdown vs control mice from S1-Tr (0.35±0.13 vs 2.25±0.33 per 100μm dendrite) and piriform cortex (0.30±0.15 vs 2.50±0.19 per 100μm dendrite). Learning-induced hippocampal-barrel cortex connections also disappear with neuroligin-3 knockdown.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C86 demonstrate the molecular mechanism underlying synapse formation using morphological analysis after neuroligin-3 knockdown. Statistical analyses are appropriate (p<0.01, one-way ANOVA) with adequate sample sizes (n=20 dendrites from 5 mice). The observation about hippocampal connections (C85-C86) is interesting but somewhat speculative regarding functional interpretation.

results.result: Neuroligin-3 knockdown prevents functional recruitment of associative memory neurons in barrel cortex. The percentage of neurons responding to whisker plus other signals is reduced from 68% in control to 16.7% in knockdown mice (p<0.01, χ²-test). This demonstrates that neuroligin-3-mediated synapse linkage is required for associative memory neuron recruitment.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C88 provide functional evidence complementing the morphological findings, using electrophysiology with appropriate statistical analysis (χ²-test, p<0.01). Sample sizes are adequate (n=50 neurons from 5 mice in control, n=24 neurons from 5 mice in knockdown). The dramatic reduction in multi-modal responsive neurons supports the causal role of neuroligin-3.

results.result: Increased retrograde EGFP labeling is detected in hippocampal CA1-CA3 areas in PSG mice compared to UPSG mice, suggesting the hippocampus may strengthen memories through increased synapse innervation to barrel cortex after memory formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C40 present an interesting observation about hippocampal connectivity, but the functional interpretation (C40) is speculative. While the anatomical observation appears valid, no quantification is provided, and the causal role of hippocampus in memory strengthening is not directly tested. This remains a hypothesis requiring further investigation.

results.result: The study proposes a conceptual framework where associative memory neurons are recruited through neuroligin-3-mediated synapse formation to encode multiple associated signals. Learning involves coactivation of sensory cortices, memory formation involves activity-dependent interconnection formation, and memory retrieval involves reactivation of associative memory neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C8, C92-C96 present the study's conceptual framework, which is well-supported by the experimental data presented in other claim groups. While some elements are speculative (C1, C2, C94-C96), the overall framework is substantiated by the behavioral, anatomical, and molecular evidence. This represents a synthesis of the findings rather than independent results.

results.result: The study builds on established knowledge about associative learning and memory, cortical encoding of sensory modalities, Hebbian plasticity principles, and molecular mechanisms of synapse formation. Previous studies have identified associative memory neurons with morphological interconnections and functional encoding capabilities.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C17, C35-C38, C72-C73, C89-C91 represent background knowledge and literature review supported by appropriate citations. These establish the scientific context for the current work. While not original findings, they are accurately represented and properly attributed to prior research.

results.result: The study uses C57BL/6JThy1-YFP mice with genetically labeled glutamatergic neurons and employs AAV-mediated anterograde (AAV2/8-CMV-tdTomato) and retrograde (AAV/retro-CMV-EGFP) viral tracing to map neural circuits.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C99 describe established methodological approaches that are well-documented in the literature and appropriately cited. These are standard techniques in the field and their application is properly described. The methods are appropriate for the research questions.

results.result: Associative learning by pairing whisker stimulation with olfactory, tail, and gustatory signals leads to reciprocal retrieval of associated signals in trained mice (PSG) but not in unpaired control mice (UPSG). Behavioral data show that olfactory, tail, and gustatory stimuli can induce whisker motion in PSG mice, and conversely, whisker stimulation can evoke olfactory avoidance, tail swing, and tongue licking responses.
results.evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly affirm this finding. Reviewer 1 states the manuscript provides 'solid support for this plasticity being a basis for cross-modal associative memories.' Reviewer 2 notes they 'use behavioral protocols to link stimuli to whisker movement' and Reviewer 3 identifies this as 'the key finding' that 'after associative learning, barrel neurons respond to other multi-model stimulations.' The behavioral data are accepted without critique.

results.result: Barrel cortical neurons interconnect with piriform, S1-Tr, and gustatory cortical neurons after associative learning. Anatomical tracing shows increased axon projections and synapse contacts between the barrel cortex and these sensory cortices in PSG mice compared to UPSG mice, with bidirectional connectivity demonstrated through anterograde and retrograde viral tracing.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly support the anatomical findings. Reviewer 2 states 'Based on anatomical correlations, they suggest that structural plasticity between different areas can be linked to training.' Reviewer 3 notes 'They found these barrel cortical neurons interconnect with other structures including piriform cortex, S1-Tr and gustatory cortical neurons.' The structural plasticity data are treated as convincing evidence for the connectivity claims.

results.result: Barrel cortical neurons in mice that experienced associative learning become functionally recruited as associative memory neurons that encode multiple modalities. Electrophysiological recordings show 64.3% of barrel cortical neurons in PSG mice respond to whisker plus olfactory, tail, and/or gustatory signals compared to 22% in UPSG mice, with increased spike frequencies to non-whisker stimuli.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the functional recruitment findings. Reviewer 2 states 'they provide electrophysiological correlates that link to behavior and structure.' Reviewer 3 notes the data are 'in general supporting their conclusions' and identifies the functional responses as part of the key findings. No concerns are raised about the electrophysiological evidence.

results.result: With the barrel cortex as a hub, indirect activation occurs among piriform, gustatory, and S1-Tr cortices for second-order associative memory. Behavioral experiments show that olfactory, tail, and gustatory stimuli can trigger cross-modal responses among each other in PSG mice, bypassing direct whisker stimulation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers implicitly accept this finding as part of the overall contribution. Reviewer 2 notes they 'discover that the barrel cortex can be a hub for associations,' directly supporting the hub concept. Reviewer 3 states the study 'reveals novel modalities associative learning involving multiple functionally connective cortical regions,' which encompasses the indirect activation mechanism. No specific critiques are raised about the second-order memory claims.

results.result: Neuroligin-3 knockdown in the barrel cortex downregulates associative memory formation and the recruitment of associative memory neurons. Behavioral, anatomical, and electrophysiological data show that neuroligin-3 knockdown reduces cross-modal responses, synapse contacts, and multi-modal neuronal encoding compared to scramble controls.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly affirm the neuroligin-3 findings. Reviewer 2 states 'Knock-down of nlg3 abolishes plasticity and learning.' Reviewer 3 notes 'Neuroligin 3 mediated the recruitment of associative memory neurons' and 'knockdown Neuroligin 3 in the barrel cortex suppressed the associative memory cell recruitment.' The causal molecular mechanism is accepted as a key contribution.

results.result: Associative memory neurons are recruited as the core cellular substrate to memorize multiple associated signals through neuroligin-3-mediated synapse formation. The authors propose a conceptual framework where associative learning involves coactivation of sensory cortices, memory formation involves activity-dependent interconnections, and retrieval involves reactivation of associative memory neurons.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the overall conceptual framework and conclusions. Reviewer 1 calls it 'a valuable contribution supporting structural and functional brain plasticity' for associative memories. Reviewer 2 states 'This study provides an important contribution as to how multi-modal associations can be formed across cortical regions.' Reviewer 3 concludes 'Data presented are in general supporting their conclusions.' The integrative model is treated as a valid synthesis of the findings.

results.result: Background claims establishing the theoretical framework, prior literature, and methodological approaches. These include established knowledge about cortical encoding of sensory modalities, previous findings on associative memory neurons, the role of neuroligin-3 in synapse formation, and technical details of viral tracing methods.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not question these background and methodological claims. The theoretical framework is implicitly accepted as reviewers engage with the novel findings without challenging the foundational assumptions or methods. These claims provide necessary context but are not the focus of reviewer evaluation.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluations strongly support the behavioral evidence for cross-modal associative memory (C18-C34). OpenEval emphasizes statistical rigor and sample sizes, while peer reviewers describe it as 'solid support' and 'the key finding.' Complete agreement on this core behavioral finding.

Both support anatomical connectivity findings (C41-C48). OpenEval focuses on viral tracing methodology and quantification, while peer reviewers accept the structural plasticity data as convincing evidence. Peer R2 also includes convergent synapse claims (C49-C56) that OpenEval separates into R3.

OpenEval R3 addresses convergent synapse innervation (C49-C56) with detailed methodological assessment. Peer R2 groups these anatomical findings together with bidirectional connectivity (C41-C48), treating all structural plasticity evidence as a unified finding supporting training-linked connectivity.

Both strongly support functional recruitment of associative memory neurons (C57-C63) through electrophysiology. OpenEval provides detailed statistical validation, while peer reviewers accept the electrophysiological correlates linking behavior and structure without specific concerns.

Both support second-order associative memory and hub function (C64-C71). OpenEval emphasizes cross-modal responses bypassing whisker signal with statistical detail, while peer reviewers implicitly accept this as part of the barrel cortex hub discovery without specific critique.

Both strongly support neuroligin-3 knockdown behavioral findings (C74-C80). OpenEval emphasizes causal evidence with controls and statistics, while peer reviewers explicitly affirm this as a key contribution. Peer R5 also includes morphological (C83-C86) and electrophysiological (C87-C88) neuroligin-3 data that OpenEval separates.

OpenEval R7 addresses morphological mechanism of neuroligin-3 (C83-C86) with some speculation noted about hippocampal connections. Peer R5 groups all neuroligin-3 evidence together (behavioral, morphological, functional) as a unified causal molecular mechanism finding.

OpenEval R8 addresses functional electrophysiology after neuroligin-3 knockdown (C87-C88), noting dramatic reduction in multi-modal neurons. Peer R5 includes this as part of comprehensive neuroligin-3 evidence, accepting the causal role without separating functional from structural effects.

OpenEval rates hippocampal connectivity claims (C39-C40) as UNCERTAIN due to speculation and lack of quantification/causal testing. Peer R2 includes these claims within accepted anatomical findings without expressing concern, treating them as part of structural plasticity evidence.

Both support the overall conceptual framework and synthesis (C1-C2, C8, C92-C96). OpenEval notes some elements are speculative but substantiated by experimental data, while peer reviewers accept it as a valuable contribution and valid synthesis without qualification.

Both accept background literature and context claims (C9-C17, C35-C38, C72-C73, C89-C91). OpenEval notes these are properly attributed prior research, while peer reviewers implicitly accept without challenge. Both treat these as necessary context rather than novel findings requiring evaluation.

Both accept methodological claims (C97-C99) as established, well-documented approaches. OpenEval explicitly notes they are standard techniques appropriately applied, while peer reviewers do not question methods, implicitly accepting them as part of the foundational framework.
